title: HVAC Distributor Vetting
result: 2 of 3 shortlisted distributors eliminated; 47 qualified buyer signals generated
summary: How a European HVAC Manufacturer Validated Distributor Claims in Nigeria Before Committing Capital.
image_alt: Rooftop commercial HVAC units on a city building
challenge: The client had been approached by three Nigerian distributors claiming established HVAC networks. They had no way to verify whether these partners actually had field sales teams, real customer relationships, or just procurement contacts. Committing to a distribution agreement without validation risked years of poor market coverage.

process.title: Understand
process.description: Mapped the addressable buyer universe across hospitals, hotels, and commercial property developers in Lagos and Abuja (312 target accounts).

process.title: Validate
process.description: Conducted structured interviews with each distributor’s referenced customers. Simultaneously ran direct outbound demand testing via LinkedIn and email to the mapped account list to gauge independent market appetite.

process.title: Connect
process.description: Developed a distributor scoring framework covering territory coverage, technical capability, existing brand conflicts, and CRM/lead tracking maturity.

process.title: Execute
process.description: Presented validated findings with a recommended path.

validation: Distributor validation: Distributor A (strongest claimed network): only 4 of 12 referenced customers confirmed an active purchasing relationship. Distributor B: 9 of 10 references confirmed. Distributor C: no verifiable field sales activity. The 47 qualified opportunities were buyers who confirmed active HVAC sourcing needs within 6 months.
outcome: The client selected Distributor B for a structured trial agreement with staged exclusivity: 6-month territory-based exclusivity contingent on monthly pipeline reporting and minimum quarterly order thresholds. Distributors A and C were disqualified. The 47 qualified buyer signals were handed over as a warm pipeline for the new distributor to work, with a 90-day follow-up protocol.
quote: We were about to sign with the biggest name in the room. P23 showed us that the name meant nothing without field activity. We saved ourselves at least two years of slow sales.
cta_heading: If you’re evaluating African distributors based on presentations rather than verified field activity, you’re making a decision on incomplete information.
cta_description: Book a Discovery Call to design your distributor validation process.

title: HVAC Market Entry
sector: HVAC Equipment Manufacturer (Commercial AC & Cold Room Systems)

result: 2 distributors signed; 15 qualified opportunities in first 90 days
summary: How an Asian HVAC Brand Built Verified Distributor Coverage in Two East African Markets Before Committing Inventory.
image_alt: Two business partners meeting at a conference table for distributor verification
challenge: The client had no African presence but wanted to enter East Africa. They had received inbound interest from two Nairobi-based companies claiming to be “HVAC distributors.” However, the client had no framework for evaluating whether these were genuine field sales operations or just order-takers with a shopfront. They needed structured market entry, not opportunistic entry.

process.title: Understand
process.description: Compared Kenya and Tanzania market entry viability using infrastructure spend, import duty structures, and competitive intensity. Kenya scored higher for speed-to-market.

process.title: Validate
process.description: Expanded the distributor search beyond the two inbound inquiries. Sourced 11 additional candidates through industry networks, trade show exhibitor lists, and refrigeration contractor associations.

process.title: Connect
process.description: Ran a structured vetting process including company registration verification, site visits, reference customer interviews, and field sales capability assessment (number of sales staff, territory coverage, lead tracking methods).

process.title: Execute
process.description: Negotiated a trial order structure and 6-month performance review clause with the two selected distributors.

validation: Vetting elimination: 4 candidates eliminated for having no field sales staff (order-takers only); 2 eliminated for representing competing HVAC brands with exclusive agreements. First 90 days post-signing: Distributor 1 (Kenya) generated 9 qualified opportunities; Distributor 2 (Tanzania) generated 6. Both distributors required Factory 23 setup and training before consistent lead logging began (weeks 3–4).
outcome: Coolair Systems entered Kenya and Tanzania with a staged distribution model: trial order quantities with a 6-month performance review before full container commitments. Both distributors are now operating with Factory 23 for pipeline visibility. The client has clear data on field activity for the first time in any African market.
cta_heading: If you’re receiving inbound distributor interest in Africa but have no way to separate serious field operations from order-takers, you need a structured vetting process.

title: Industrial Equipment Market Entry
result: Distributor signed in 5 months; first order within 60 days of agreement
summary: How a UK Equipment Manufacturer Selected Ghana Over Nigeria for First African Entry and Why It Mattered.
image_alt: Industrial generators and power equipment in a plant hall
challenge: CmpPower wanted to enter West Africa but was paralysed by the choice between Nigeria (large market, high complexity) and Ghana (smaller market, reportedly easier). They had no African operating experience and were receiving conflicting advice. They needed a structured comparison, not anecdotes.

process.title: Understand
process.description: Built a market entry scorecard comparing Nigeria and Ghana across 8 criteria: import duty structure, ease of company registration, distributor availability, infrastructure quality, currency stability, competitive intensity, addressable customer universe size, and time-to-first-revenue estimate.

process.title: Validate
process.description: Conducted 14 distributor interviews across both markets. Assessed field sales capability, existing brand portfolios, and willingness to commit to a trial structure.

process.title: Connect
process.description: Selected Ghana as the recommended entry market based on faster time-to-revenue, a simpler import process, lower distributor conflict risk, and existing distributor candidates with strong technical sales teams.

process.title: Execute
process.description: Negotiated a staged exclusivity agreement: 12-month exclusive territory rights in Ghana, contingent on minimum quarterly order volumes and monthly pipeline reporting via Factory 23.

validation: Scorecard outcome: Ghana ranked higher on 5 of 8 criteria (time-to-revenue, import simplicity, distributor quality, currency stability, ease of registration); Nigeria ranked higher on market size and long-term ceiling. Distributor candidates: 8 interviewed across both markets → 3 shortlisted in Ghana → 1 signed. First order placed 60 days after signing: a ₵180,000 initial order for demonstration units and trial inventory. Visits, opportunities, and orders above cover the first 90 days.
outcome: CmpPower entered Ghana with a low-risk, verifiable structure: staged exclusivity, trial order quantities, and mandatory pipeline reporting. They now have an operating base in West Africa with data on actual field activity and sales performance. Nigeria remains on the 18-month roadmap, with the Ghana operation serving as the regional proof point.
cta_heading: If you’re comparing African markets on size alone, you’re missing the criteria that determine whether you’ll actually get to revenue.
cta_description: Book a Discovery Call to build a market entry scorecard for your product.

title: Multi-Market Demand Testing
result: 1 market recommended for entry; 2 deprioritised based on buyer signal data
summary: How a European Equipment Manufacturer Tested Demand in Three African Markets Before Committing to Any.
image_alt: Industrial generators and power equipment in a plant hall
challenge: Liftmasters’ board had approved “Africa expansion” but wanted evidence before committing capital. They had no African presence and no clear view of which market offered the best demand signal relative to entry cost. They needed a go/no-go case for at least one market, not a continent-wide strategy document.

process.title: Understand
process.description: Defined the target buyer profile: manufacturing plants, warehouses, and logistics companies using or planning to acquire material handling equipment.

process.title: Validate
process.description: Ran parallel outbound demand testing in Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa. Identical messaging and an identical offer (technical consultation + equipment assessment), sent to matched buyer profiles in each market.

process.title: Connect
process.description: Tracked response rates, qualification rates, and buyer intent signals (stated timelines, budget confirmation, decision-maker access).

process.title: Execute
process.description: Delivered a market prioritisation recommendation with the underlying signal data.

validation: Accounts contacted: 150 per market. Response rates: Nigeria 14%, Kenya 9%, South Africa 7%. Qualified opportunities (confirmed active need within 6 months): Nigeria 21, Kenya 9, South Africa 4. Decision-maker access: in Nigeria 67% of respondents were operations or procurement decision-makers, against 44% in Kenya and 38% in South Africa.
outcome: The board approved Nigeria as the initial entry market based on demand signal strength and decision-maker access. Kenya was flagged as a secondary opportunity requiring a different channel strategy (stronger distributor dependency). South Africa was deprioritised due to lower response signal and higher competitive saturation. The 21 qualified Nigerian opportunities were handed to the sales team as a warm pipeline to pursue during market entry setup.
cta_heading: If your Africa expansion decision is based on market size reports rather than direct buyer signal, you’re guessing.
cta_description: Book a Discovery Call to design a demand testing campaign for your priority markets.

title: Regulatory & Partner Mapping
result: Full regulatory roadmap delivered; 11 distributor candidates mapped and scored
summary: How an Equipment Manufacturer Mapped Kenya’s Regulatory Pathway and Distributor Landscape in 6 Weeks.
challenge: GP Equipment wanted to enter Kenya but was blocked by uncertainty: What licences were required? What were the import procedures? Who were the credible distributors? They had received partial information from a local contact but couldn’t validate it. The lack of a clear roadmap was delaying board approval.

process.title: Understand
process.description: Compiled Kenya’s regulatory requirements for industrial equipment import and distribution: KEBS certification, import declaration forms, tax registration, and any sector-specific requirements for power equipment.

process.title: Validate
process.description: Verified each regulatory step directly through Kenyan government portals and interviews with two licensed customs agents and one KEBS-registered importer.

process.title: Connect
process.description: Mapped the distributor landscape through industry associations, trade show exhibitor lists, and LinkedIn research. Identified 11 potential distribution partners.

process.title: Execute
process.description: Scored each distributor on field sales staff count, territory coverage, existing brand conflicts, technical capability, and reference customer validation.

validation: Regulatory pathway: 7 required steps, an estimated 4–6 week timeline for full compliance, and an approximate cost range for each step. Distributor mapping: 11 candidates identified → 6 contacted → 4 provided detailed capability information → 2 recommended for final evaluation. The top-ranked candidate had 7 field sales staff, 3 technical support engineers, existing relationships with 40+ industrial buyers, and no directly competing generator brand. Risk flag: one candidate had an undisclosed exclusive agreement with a European competitor, which only surfaced through direct verification and would have disqualified them.
outcome: The client received a complete Kenya entry roadmap: regulatory steps, timeline, cost estimates, and two validated distributor candidates with full scoring data. Board approval was granted within 2 weeks of receiving the report. The client is now in negotiation with the top-ranked distributor using a trial order structure.
cta_heading: If regulatory uncertainty or distributor opacity is blocking your African market entry decision, you need structured mapping, not more anecdotes.
cta_description: Book a Discovery Call to build your market entry roadmap.

title: Agricultural After-Sales Network
result: Service network established; 45% reduction in downtime complaints
summary: How an Agricultural Machinery Manufacturer Built an After-Sales Service Network in Tanzania.
image_alt: Tractors and harvesters working an agricultural field at sunset
challenge: AgriMech had sold equipment into Tanzania through a local distributor, but after-sales support was almost non-existent. Customers complained about long downtimes, lack of spare parts, and no local technical support. This was damaging the brand and limiting repeat sales. The distributor had no service infrastructure.

process.title: Understand

process.title: Validate
process.description: Interviewed 15 existing customers to quantify downtime impact and identify priority service needs.

process.title: Connect
process.description: Identified and vetted two local technical service providers with agricultural machinery experience.

process.title: Execute
process.description: Set up a service network with spare parts consignment stock, a technician training programme, and a service request tracking system integrated with Factory 23 for visibility.

validation: Customer interviews: 15 customers reported an average downtime of 12 days per breakdown. Service network: 2 service providers contracted and 4 technicians trained, with an initial consignment stock of 45 critical parts. Average downtime fell to 6.5 days within 6 months (a 45% reduction). Repeat sales: 3 customers who had delayed purchases over service concerns placed new orders within 8 months.
outcome: AgriMech now has a functioning after-sales service network in Tanzania. Customer complaints dropped significantly. The distributor is now selling with confidence, knowing that service support exists. Repeat sales are increasing.
